notes.definition: Carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻) are identified by adding a dilute acid. Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas, which turns limewater milky.
explanation: To test a substance for carbonate ions, add a few cm³ of dilute acid, such as hydrochloric acid, to the solid or solution in a test tube. If a carbonate is present there will be effervescence (fizzing) as carbon dioxide gas is produced. To prove that the gas is carbon dioxide, pass it through limewater using a bung and delivery tube, or draw the gas up with a dropping pipette and bubble it into limewater. Carbon dioxide turns the limewater milky (cloudy).

Fizzing alone is not enough to identify a carbonate, because metals such as magnesium and zinc also fizz with acids, producing hydrogen. Hydrogen does not affect limewater, so the limewater step is what confirms the carbonate. This test can be used on soluble carbonates such as sodium carbonate solution, and on insoluble solid carbonates such as calcium carbonate or copper(II) carbonate.

The general reaction is: carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide. For example, Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) and CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). In terms of ions (Higher tier), every carbonate reacts in the same way: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂. The metal ion is a spectator, which is why this test identifies only the carbonate ion. The milkiness in limewater is insoluble calcium carbonate formed from the carbon dioxide.

The carbonate test is part of required practical 7. It is also the reason why acid is added first in the halide and sulfate tests: carbonate ions would also form precipitates with silver nitrate and with barium chloride, giving false positive results, so the acid is added to react with and remove any carbonate ions as carbon dioxide.
keyFacts: Test: add dilute acid; carbonates fizz (effervesce).
Bubble the gas through limewater: carbon dioxide turns it milky.
Carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Fizzing alone is not proof: metals fizz with acid too, giving hydrogen.
Works for soluble and insoluble carbonates.
Acid is added before the halide and sulfate tests to remove carbonate ions.

keyTerms.definition: The negative ion CO₃²⁻, found in compounds such as calcium carbonate and sodium carbonate.
Fizzing caused by bubbles of gas being produced in a liquid.
Calcium hydroxide solution, which turns milky with carbon dioxide.
A negatively charged ion, such as CO₃²⁻, Cl⁻ or SO₄²⁻.
An acid with a low concentration of dissolved acid in water, such as dilute hydrochloric acid.

workedExamples.title: Testing an unknown powder
workedExamples.question: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a green powder. It fizzes and the gas turns limewater milky. A blue-green solution forms. What is the negative ion, and what could the powder be?
steps: Fizzing with acid and a gas that turns limewater milky shows carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide from an acid reaction shows carbonate ions.
A green powder giving a blue-green solution suggests copper(II) ions.
workedExamples.answer: Carbonate ion; the powder could be copper(II) carbonate.

workedExamples.title: Writing the equation
workedExamples.question: Write a balanced symbol equation for potassium carbonate reacting with dilute nitric acid.
steps: Two K on the left, so 2KNO₃ on the right.
That needs 2 NO₃, so 2HNO₃; check H: 2 on each side.

workedExamples.title: Carbonate or metal?
workedExamples.question: Two grey powders both fizz with dilute acid. Powder A's gas turns limewater milky; powder B's gas pops with a burning splint. Identify what each contains.
steps: Gas that turns limewater milky is carbon dioxide, so A contains a carbonate.
Gas that pops is hydrogen, made by a metal reacting with acid.
workedExamples.answer: A is a carbonate; B is a metal (such as zinc or iron powder).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think fizzing with acid proves a carbonate is present.
misconceptions.right: In fact metals also fizz with acid (producing hydrogen). The gas must turn limewater milky to confirm carbon dioxide and so a carbonate.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write that carbonates and acids give 'salt and hydrogen'.
misconceptions.right: In fact the products are a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the carbonate test identifies the whole compound.
misconceptions.right: In fact it identifies only the carbonate ion; the metal ion needs a flame test or sodium hydroxide.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think only soluble carbonates can be tested.
misconceptions.right: In fact insoluble carbonates such as calcium carbonate also react with acid and fizz.

realWorld: Geologists drop dilute acid on rocks in the field: limestone and marble (calcium carbonate) fizz.
Indigestion tablets contain carbonates that neutralise excess stomach acid, releasing carbon dioxide.
Baking powder releases carbon dioxide when its carbonate component reacts with an acid, making cakes rise.
higherTier: Ionic equation for any carbonate with acid: CO₃²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) → H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). For a solid carbonate: CaCO₃(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
separateOnlyContent: The carbonate ion test as part of identifying ions (required practical 7) is in separate Chemistry only (8462).
examTips: Give both stages: 'add dilute acid' and 'gas turns limewater milky'. Fizzing alone scores at most one mark.
Remember the products: salt + water + carbon dioxide.
If asked why acid is added first in halide or sulfate tests, answer 'to remove carbonate ions, which would also form a precipitate'.
Use the word 'effervescence' or 'fizzing' for the observation, not 'carbon dioxide is produced'.
summary: Carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Fizzing alone could be hydrogen from a metal.
Acid removes carbonate before halide and sulfate tests.

flashcards.front: How do you test for carbonate ions?
flashcards.back: Add dilute acid; bubble any gas through limewater.
Fizzing; the gas turns limewater milky (carbon dioxide).

flashcards.front: Why is fizzing alone not enough?
flashcards.back: Metals also fizz with acids, producing hydrogen.

flashcards.front: Why add acid before the halide or sulfate test?
flashcards.back: To remove carbonate ions, which would give a false precipitate.

flashcards.front: Can insoluble carbonates be tested this way?
flashcards.back: Yes, for example solid calcium carbonate fizzes with acid.

flashcards.front: Which practical includes the carbonate test?

questions.question: What is added to a sample to test for carbonate ions?
markScheme: 1 mark: Dilute acid
questions.explanation: Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide. The others test for metal ions, halides and sulfates.

questions.question: What is produced when a carbonate reacts with a dilute acid?
markScheme: 1 mark: Salt, water and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Metal oxide + CO₂ is thermal decomposition.

questions.question: Which observation confirms the gas from a carbonate test is carbon dioxide?
markScheme: 1 mark: It turns limewater milky
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky. The others are tests for oxygen, chlorine and hydrogen.

questions.question: A powder fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid, but the gas does not affect limewater. What could the powder be?
markScheme: 1 mark: Magnesium metal
questions.explanation: Magnesium reacts with acid to give hydrogen, which does not turn limewater milky. All carbonates give carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Which equation is correctly balanced?
markScheme: 1 mark: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂
questions.explanation: Sodium carbonate is Na₂CO₃, giving 2NaCl; 2HCl provides the 2 H for water.

questions.question: Which is the ionic equation for a carbonate reacting with an acid?
markScheme: 1 mark: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂
questions.explanation: Two H⁺ ions react with one carbonate ion to give water and carbon dioxide; charges balance (2− + 2+ = 0).

questions.question: Why is dilute nitric acid added before silver nitrate in the test for halide ions?
options: To remove carbonate ions, which would also form a precipitate
To change the colour of the precipitate
markScheme: 1 mark: To remove carbonate ions, which would also form a precipitate
questions.explanation: Carbonate ions would also give a precipitate with silver ions, so they are removed as carbon dioxide first.

questions.question: A white solid fizzes with dilute acid and the gas turns limewater milky. It gives a yellow flame. What is the solid?
markScheme: 1 mark: Sodium carbonate
questions.explanation: Yellow flame shows sodium; CO₂ with acid shows carbonate.

questions.question: Which statement explains why every carbonate gives the same result in this test?
options: It is the carbonate ion that reacts with hydrogen ions, and the metal ion is a spectator
The metal ion reacts with the acid
markScheme: 1 mark: It is the carbonate ion that reacts with hydrogen ions, and the metal ion is a spectator
questions.explanation: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂ for every carbonate; the metal ion does not take part. Many carbonates (such as CaCO₃) are insoluble.

questions.question: What word describes the fizzing seen when a carbonate reacts with acid?
markScheme: 1 mark: Effervescence
questions.explanation: Effervescence means fizzing from gas bubbles.

questions.question: Describe the test for carbonate ions and give the result.
markScheme: 1 mark: add dilute acid; (fizzing) and pass gas into limewater
1 mark: limewater turns milky
questions.explanation: The limewater step confirms carbon dioxide, which shows the carbonate.

questions.question: Name the gas produced when calcium carbonate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Explain why seeing fizzing when an acid is added does not prove that a carbonate is present.
markScheme: 1 mark: other substances (for example reactive metals) also fizz with acid, producing hydrogen
1 mark: the gas must be shown to turn limewater milky to confirm carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Only the limewater result is specific to carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction of calcium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct formulae
1 mark: balanced with 2HCl
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ needs two Cl⁻, so 2HCl react.

questions.question: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction between sodium carbonate solution and dilute sulfuric acid.
markScheme: 1 mark: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂
1 mark: correct state symbols
questions.explanation: Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻ are spectator ions, so the ionic equation is the same as for any soluble carbonate with any acid.

questions.question: A student adds dilute acid to a solid and wants to test the gas with limewater, but has no delivery tube. Suggest how the student could still test the gas.
markScheme: 1 mark: use a (clean) dropping pipette to draw up gas from above the reaction
1 mark: bubble it into a test tube of limewater and look for milkiness
questions.explanation: This is a common technique in required practical 7 when small amounts are used.

questions.question: Explain why barium chloride solution is added only after hydrochloric acid when testing for sulfate ions in a sample that might also contain carbonate ions.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbonate ions would react with barium ions to form a white precipitate (barium carbonate)
1 mark: acid removes the carbonate ions as carbon dioxide, so any white precipitate must be barium sulfate
questions.explanation: The acid prevents a false positive result.

questions.question: What colour change shows that carbon dioxide is present in limewater?
markScheme: 1 mark: clear/colourless to milky/cloudy
questions.explanation: A white precipitate of calcium carbonate forms.

questions.question: Required practical 7: describe how a student could show that a white powder contains carbonate ions. Include the apparatus and the expected results.
markScheme: Indicative content: place a small amount of the powder in a test tube
Add a few cm³ of dilute hydrochloric (or nitric) acid
Fizzing/effervescence seen
Quickly fit a bung with delivery tube into a second tube containing limewater (or use a pipette to transfer gas)
Limewater turns milky, showing carbon dioxide, so carbonate present
Safety: eye protection; dilute acid is an irritant
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear method with apparatus, both observations and conclusion
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): adding acid or limewater result mentioned
questions.explanation: Both observations (fizzing and milky limewater) and a practical way of transferring the gas are needed.

questions.question: A student is given three unlabelled powders: sodium carbonate, sodium chloride and zinc powder. Describe how the student could use tests from this topic to identify each powder, giving results. Include balanced equations for any reactions that produce gases, and explain why the limewater test is needed.
markScheme: Indicative content: add dilute hydrochloric acid to each in separate tubes
Sodium carbonate: fizzes; gas turns limewater milky (CO₂)
Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂
Zinc: fizzes; gas does not turn limewater milky; burns with a pop (H₂)
Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
Sodium chloride: no fizzing
Confirm chloride: dissolve, add dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate: white precipitate
Flame test gives yellow for both sodium compounds
Limewater needed because both carbonate and zinc fizz; only CO₂ turns limewater milky
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all three identified with correct tests, results and both equations, and clear explanation of limewater's role
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least two identified with some correct equations or explanation
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one test or result described
questions.explanation: The best answers use acid to divide the powders, then limewater and the burning splint to distinguish carbon dioxide from hydrogen.

questions.question: Which of these compounds would NOT produce carbon dioxide when dilute acid is added?
markScheme: 1 mark: Potassium chloride
questions.explanation: Only carbonates produce CO₂ with acids. Potassium chloride contains no carbonate ions.

questions.question: Indigestion tablet A fizzes in dilute hydrochloric acid and the gas turns limewater milky. What does this show about tablet A?
markScheme: 1 mark: It contains a carbonate
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide from an acid reaction shows a carbonate.

questions.question: Dilute sulfuric acid is added to a green solid. It fizzes, the gas turns limewater milky and a blue solution forms. Adding sodium hydroxide to the blue solution gives a blue precipitate. Name the green solid.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbonate (CO₂ turns limewater milky)
1 mark: copper(II) (blue precipitate with NaOH): copper(II) carbonate
questions.explanation: Combining the negative-ion and positive-ion tests identifies the compound.

questions.question: Predict the products when lithium carbonate reacts with dilute nitric acid, and write a balanced equation.
markScheme: 1 mark: lithium nitrate, water and carbon dioxide
1 mark: Li₂CO₃ + 2HNO₃ → 2LiNO₃ + H₂O + CO₂
questions.explanation: Nitric acid gives nitrate salts. Li⁺ is 1+ so the carbonate is Li₂CO₃.

questions.question: In the carbonate test, why should the delivery tube be placed in the limewater straight after the acid is added?
options: So that the carbon dioxide produced is not lost before it reaches the limewater
To keep air out of the acid
To make the acid react faster
markScheme: 1 mark: So that the carbon dioxide produced is not lost before it reaches the limewater
questions.explanation: The reaction is fast, so the gas must be captured quickly for a clear result.

questions.question: What is the formula of the carbonate ion?
markScheme: 1 mark: CO₃²⁻
questions.explanation: The carbonate ion is CO₃²⁻ (one carbon, three oxygens, 2− charge). CO₂ is carbon dioxide, the gas produced in the test.
